summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used for text-based emotional support. However, general-purpose LLMs may not consistently recognize emotional cues, adapt supportive strategies to contexts, or generate responses aligned with psychologically informed communication. The limited availability of large-scale, structured Chinese counseling data further constrains the development of models for context-sensitive emotional support. Objective: We developed and evaluated YuanChat, a family of specialized LLMs for context-sensitive emotional support; assessed whether E-URIAL improved response quality; and compared YuanChat with base LLMs. Methods: We constructed 2 datasets from anonymized real-world counseling sessions: ECD-3 (104,897 counselor response turns) for fine-tuning and (9413 manually annotated counselor responses). Annotations covered emotional support conversation stages (exploration, comfort, and action), counseling techniques (clarification, support, and challenge), and empathic effects. We developed 2 YuanChat variants using GLM-4-9B-Chat and Huozi 3.5 as backbone models using parameter-efficient fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We then developed E-URIAL, an inference-time framework combining predicted emotion and support strategy labels with retrieved labeled exemplars. Given the dialogue history through the help seeker’s latest utterance, each model generated a counselor-style response. We compared YuanChat with GPT-4, ERNIE 4.0, CharacterGLM, GLM-4-9B-Chat, and Huozi 3.5. The evaluation comprised (1) automatic evaluation on in-domain and external datasets, assessing empathy identification and empathic expression; (2) evaluation of empathy-related situational reasoning using an expert-developed multiple-choice benchmark; (3) evaluation by clinical experts (n=8) of empathic attunement, support strategy appropriateness, perceived helpfulness, and safety and professional boundary adherence; and (4) a complementary evaluation by volunteer master’s students in clinical and counseling psychology (n=50) of response fluency, empathy, and perceived helpfulness. Results: Fine-tuning increased YuanChat-Huozi3.5’s empathic expression score from 0.57 to 0.68; empathy identification score increased from 0.54 to 0.59. In expert evaluation, YuanChat-Huozi3.5 received a higher empathic attunement score than the base Huozi3.5 model (1.279 vs 0.327; mean difference 0.952, 95% CI 0.746‐1.152). Using professional counselor responses as the reference, the mean differences for YuanChat-Huozi3.5 were 0.148, 0.079, 0.039, and 0.002 in empathic attunement, supportive appropriateness, perceived helpfulness, and safety and professional boundary adherence, respectively. No statistically significant differences were detected between YuanChat-Huozi3.5 and the counselor references (all Holm-adjusted ≥.29). Higher scores were observed when E-URIAL was applied. When E-URIAL was applied with 3 retrieved exemplars, YuanChat-Huozi3.5 achieved an empathy identification score of 0.69 versus 0.59 without E-URIAL, an empathic expression score of 0.79 versus 0.68, and a perceived helpfulness score of 0.74 versus 0.61. Conclusions: The findings indicate that fine-tuning on real-world counseling data and annotating models with structured emotional support labels improved context-sensitive empathic responding in LLMs. Without updating model parameters, E-URIAL further improved empathy identification and empathic expression across multiple models. Together, these methods provide a scalable, theory-informed approach to enhancing the emotional support capabilities of LLMs.
title: A Multistage Fine-Tuning and Empathy Alignment Approach for an Emotional Support Dialogue System: Development and Evaluation Study

summary: Background: AI is a broad field encompassing various techniques, which include algorithms that learn from data to perform automated tasks without explicit human programming. Public health aims to protect and improve the health of communities and populations at the local, regional, national, and global levels, but it typically has limited resources. While AI may lead to improved efficiency or effectiveness of public health interventions, the adoption of AI interventions should be informed by evidence of effective use in practice. Objective: This review aims to summarize how AI-assisted interventions are currently used by public health professionals. Methods: We conducted a scoping review to identify the current uses of AI in public health. We searched MEDLINE (Ovid), Embase (Ovid), Web of Science (Core Collection), and Scopus for relevant reports published between January 1, 2020, and July 24, 2025. Two reviewers independently screened reports. Eligible reports were primary studies (experimental or observational), commentaries, and editorials that discussed how AI tools have been used in practice in public health contexts relevant to high-income countries, excluding outbreaks. Data were extracted by one reviewer and checked by a second. Results: We screened 5400 records and 155 full texts, including 8 reports. These reports discussed a variety of uses of AI tools across public health domains: 3 reports used chatbots in different settings, 1 report used machine learning to forecast health service demand, 2 reports used AI for symptom checking, and 2 reports used AI for evidence synthesis. While assessing the effectiveness of AI tools for public health was beyond the scope of this review, and most reports did not robustly evaluate effectiveness, the evidence for the effectiveness of AI tools was nonetheless mixed. One report described a chatbot that users found helpful, while another found a specific chatbot to be ineffective, highlighting its potential to undermine trust in the organization that developed it. Another report highlighted both benefits and drawbacks of a large language model used to communicate with socially isolated individuals. The main finding of this review was that even with a comprehensive search across multiple databases, there were few reports of how AI tools are being used in practice in public health contexts. Conclusions: The lack of evidence from public health practice, excluding outbreaks, makes it difficult to know which uses of AI, if any, would be useful to incorporate into practice in high-income countries. In the absence of evidence, new interventions, including those using AI, should be evaluated to ensure they are effective (and cost-effective). These evaluations should be widely and accessibly disseminated to create an evidence base that other public health teams could use to inform their own decisions around AI tools.
title: The Current Roles of AI in Public Health Practice: Scoping Review

summary: Background: Addressing the burnout epidemic among health care providers remains one of the foremost challenges of modern health care systems. Past researchers have turned to passively gathered biometric data from wearable devices to identify key variables that predict burnout. However, this has resulted in limited success. Objective: This pilot and feasibility study aimed to test the feasibility and accuracy of developing an Extreme Gradient Boosting machine learning model to classify health care providers as being at higher or lower risk of burnout based on their biometric data. Methods: We conducted a 3-month pilot and feasibility study where health care providers self-reported burnout every 6 weeks and wore a Garmin Venu 3 smartwatch to collect continuous biometric data. Participants were recruited from 3 pediatric urgent care sites and an inpatient hospitalist division of a pediatric health care system. We had a final sample of 41 participants who met our inclusion criteria requiring completion of burnout measurements at 2 of the 3 time points and having worn the watch for at least 70% of the study period. Participants were asked to wear the Garmin watch continuously over the course of the study. Burnout self-report surveys were delivered via email. Our main outcome was burnout as measured using the Maslach Burnout Inventory–Human Services Survey. The measure consists of 3 subscales that together constitute burnout: emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and reduced personal efficacy. Results: First, we found evidence of feasibility for wearable watches to be used in situ for health care providers to gather data passively for the purposes of classifying burnout. A total of 82% (51/62) of participants met our criteria of wearing the watch 70% of the time, with 66% (41/62) having corresponding burnout scores to be included in analyses. Second, our machine learning model achieved strong overall performance in identifying risk of burnout, with strong sensitivity and specificity, demonstrating that biometric data collected using wearable devices can accurately predict burnout. Conclusions: Our evidence of feasibility offers promising results for a passive method of data collection to be used for classifying burnout risk in other health care settings. Furthermore, the strong performance of our machine learning model provides a foundational step toward improving an organization’s ability to respond and mitigate burnout through thoughtful intervention strategies.
title: Identifying Burnout in Pediatric Clinicians Using Wearable Biometric Data: Development and Feasibility Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Digital health interventions, including mobile health apps, increasingly complement outpatient mental health care. In Germany, certified digital health applications (DiGA [Digitale Gesundheitsanwendungen]) can be prescribed and reimbursed in the statutory health care system. However, real-world evidence on patient-reported use of DiGA for mental disorders remains limited. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to analyze usage patterns and experiences among DiGA users and expectations among nonusers. Among users, we examined duration of active use, self-reported completion, and experienced reasons for discontinuation; among nonusers, whether DiGA use would be an option and the perceived relevance of hypothetical reasons for discontinuation. <strong>Methods:</strong> We conducted an anonymous cross-sectional mixed-mode survey among adults insured by Techniker Krankenkasse, Germany’s largest statutory insurer. Random samples of 2000 individuals per group were invited in April 2024, and data collection ended in September 2024. Users received an activation code for a DiGA authorized for mental disorders. Nonusers had a documented diagnosis for which a DiGA was available but had no prior use. Analyses were descriptive, using available cases, frequencies, and medians with IQRs for ordinal Likert-type items. Actual and intended use were treated as distinct. Exploratory subgroup analyses were conducted. <strong>Results:</strong> Overall, 1413 participants were included in the analysis (769 of 2000 invited users; 644 of 2000 invited nonusers), with response rates of 38.5% (95% CI 36.3%-40.6%) and 32.2% (95% CI 30.2%-34.3%), respectively. A total of 840 of 1249 (67.3%; 95% CI 64.6%-69.8%) participants were female. Nonusers were older and more often lived in rural areas. Among users, 487 of 687 (70.9%; 95% CI 67.4%-74.2%) reported active use for at least 5 weeks; 409 of 700 (58.4%; 95% CI 54.7%-62.0%) reported completion of their DiGA program. The proportion of reported completions increased from 111 of 250 (44.4%; 95% CI 38.4%-50.6%) among those aged 18-40 years to 85 of 112 (75.9%; 95% CI 67.2%-82.9%) among those aged 61 years and older. The most frequently endorsed reasons for discontinuation among users reporting noncompletion were lack of motivation (151/272, 55.5%; 95% CI 49.6%-61.3%) and insufficient personalization (114/255, 44.7%; 95% CI 38.7%-50.8%). Among nonusers, the most frequently endorsed hypothetical reasons for discontinuation were mismatch with their condition (431/540, 79.8%; 95% CI 76.2%-83.0%) and technical difficulties (432/545, 79.3%; 95% CI 75.7%-82.5%). <strong>Conclusions:</strong> This study provides patient-reported real-world evidence on certified and reimbursable digital mental health interventions. Many users reported weeks of active use, but noncompletion remained common and was more frequent among younger users. Lack of motivation as a frequently reported reason for discontinuation suggests that supporting continued engagement may be important during DiGA use. Beyond Germany, these findings may support implementation of digital mental health interventions in other health care systems. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong>
title: Digital Health Applications for Mental Disorders in Germany Among Users and Nonusers on Actual and Intended Use, Self-Reported Completion, and Reasons for Discontinuation: Cross-Sectional Survey

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Digital health technologies are transforming health care by improving access, efficiency, and quality of care. However, recent studies highlight that digitalization can unintentionally reinforce or deepen existing social and health inequalities, as not all population groups benefit equally from digital progress. The concept of digital determinants of health (DDoH) has emerged to better capture how digital factors shape health opportunities and outcomes. The systematic incorporation of DDoH and other health determinants shaped by digitalization into strategic planning remains limited. As a result, health systems may lack structured approaches to identify them and anticipate their equity implications. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to identify which health determinants are considered most important in the Catalan context and to qualitatively explore their inclusion in existing regional strategies and policy frameworks in Catalonia. <strong>Methods:</strong> We conducted a modified Delphi study with experts from the Catalan health and digital ecosystem. The list of determinants was derived from a scoping review, which identified 127 determinants that emerged or changed with digitalization. Experts living and working in Catalonia, with experience in digital health, public health, health care delivery, social or DDoH, or health equity, were recruited using snowball sampling. Participants rated each determinant for importance using a 5-point Likert scale across 2 rounds, followed by a final online consensus meeting. For each determinant, the median (IQR) and the proportion of experts rating it as 4 or 5 were calculated, and items were classified into high, moderate, or low relevance according to predefined consensus criteria. <strong>Results:</strong> A total of 43 experts participated in the first Delphi round, and 31 completed the second round. Of the 127 assessed determinants, 20 (15.7%) reached high relevance for the Catalan context, including 15 digital, 4 social, and 1 political determinant. Overall, the most important determinants focused on enabling the effective and equitable use of digital health, particularly access, skills, system-level digital capacity and governance, inclusive design, and the responsible use of AI. Comparison with the original global Delphi study showed substantial overlap, but also revealed context-specific priorities. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> This study demonstrates the value of systematically contextualizing DDoH and other health determinants shaped by digitalization to inform strategic health planning in digitally mature public health systems. The findings show that international digital health agendas require regional reprioritization to reflect local infrastructure, governance arrangements and equity challenges. The results suggest that, beyond technological capacity, governance and equity considerations should become central to digital health planning. The proposed approach offers a replicable framework to support more anticipatory, coordinated and equity-oriented digital health strategies.
title: Assessing Digital Determinants of Health and Their Impact as Part of Strategic Health Planning in Catalonia: Modified Delphi Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> AI-enabled patient profiling has been proposed to organize heterogeneous patient data and support personalized nursing care and health support. Given the growing use of AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), digital phenotyping, and digital twins in health care, it is important to clarify how patient profiling has been conceptualized, applied, and evaluated in nursing-relevant contexts. <strong>Objective:</strong> This scoping review aimed to examine and report the available evidence on AI-enabled patient profiling for personalized nursing care and health support. <strong>Methods:</strong> This scoping review was conducted using the Joanna Briggs Institute methodological framework and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews). Chinese and English databases were searched from inception to May 18, 2026, including China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang Data, VIP Database, Chinese Biomedical Literature Database, PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, and Embase. Eligible studies used AI or computational intelligence methods to construct, classify, apply, validate, or evaluate patient profiles or related patient representations relevant to personalized nursing care or health support. Two reviewers independently screened records, assessed full texts, and charted data using a predefined form. Data were synthesized descriptively and narratively using an input-process-output framework. <strong>Results:</strong> A total of 61 studies were included. AI-enabled patient profiling was represented through patient profiles, patient or user personas, digital phenotypes, patient segments, clinical subtypes, digital twins, and LLM-enabled personalization. Included studies used diverse data sources, including electronic health records, nursing records, patient-reported outcomes, questionnaires, mobile app data, wearable and sensor data, engagement logs, and textual or conversational data. Common AI approaches included machine learning, clustering, deep learning, natural language processing, recommender systems, knowledge graphs, digital twin modeling, and LLMs. Applications focused on personalized education, self-management support, rehabilitation, chronic disease management, remote monitoring, decision support, follow-up care, and shared decision-making. Most studies evaluated algorithmic performance, feasibility, usability, or system development, whereas fewer studies examined profile validity, actionability, equity, workflow integration, or long-term nursing-sensitive and patient-centered outcomes. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Existing evidence positions AI-enabled patient profiling as an emerging data-to-action mechanism for personalized nursing care and health support rather than as a mature clinical intervention. Future research should strengthen conceptual clarity, validate the profile, establish explicit pathways linking profiles to actions, incorporate nurse and patient involvement, assess equity and safety, and evaluate implementation in real-world nursing settings. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong> OSF Registry mey4u; https://osf.io/mey4u
title: AI-Enabled Patient Profiling for Personalized Nursing Care and Health Support: Scoping Review

summary: Background: Emerging evidence indicates that immersive virtual reality can be used therapeutically and has demonstrated efficacy in promoting the mental health of older adults. Nevertheless, there remains a paucity of qualitative research examining the specific experiences underpinning these benefits. Objective: This study aimed to explore the perspectives of older adults who received the 12-session Immersive Virtual Reality Therapeutic Programme (IVRTP) intervention and health-related undergraduate students who delivered it as interventionists, within the context of residential care homes. Methods: A descriptive qualitative study was conducted as a qualitative exploration embedded in a multicenter randomized controlled trial evaluating the effects of IVRTP in promoting the mental health of older adults with disabilities living in residential homes. The IVRTP incorporated therapeutic elements of tourism, natural scenes, and reminiscence. Data were collected through focus group interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis. Results: Seven groups of older adults (n=28) and 3 groups of student interventionists (n=9) participated in the study. Five themes emerged: IVRTP contributes to “broadening horizons” through embracing new technology, learning new things, and engaging in new activities. Participants noted that the IVRTP provided “a realistic journey and immersive escape” from their residential home environment and mobility issues. They expressed that the IVRTP evoked “reminiscent memories” from the past and were amazed at the observed changes in tourist destinations over time. The interviews were filled with laughter and affirmations of positive emotions associated with this “joyful adventure,” although a few participants mentioned “minor discomfort,” such as eye soreness and dizziness, from wearing the head-mounted devices. Students’ accounts corroborated these themes; their meaning-making and colearning with older adults underscored the pedagogical value of authentic, community-based, intergenerational learning and reinforced the case for integrating a community practicum into the curriculum. Conclusions: Implementing an IVRTP in residential care settings, particularly for older adults with mobility limitations, is positively viewed as an accessible, enjoyable, and beneficial intervention to support psychosocial well-being. Therapeutically oriented content delivered through a structured protocol, coupled with the use of advanced IVR technology, was appreciated by both older adults and student interventionists.
title: Experiences of Immersive Virtual Reality Among Older Adults With Physical Disabilities: Qualitative Process Evaluation of a Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Medication nonadherence remains a major global health challenge, contributing to preventable disease, hospitalizations, and health care costs. Mobile health (mHealth) apps incorporating gamification and financial incentives have shown potential to improve adherence; however, most research has focused on patient perspectives, with limited understanding of how nonpatient stakeholders perceive their feasibility, risks, and implementation. Understanding nonpatient stakeholder perspectives in relation to patient viewpoints is essential for informing future policy development and establishing practical, industry-supported safeguards that protect consumers while enabling innovation. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to explore nonpatient stakeholder perspectives on the use of gamification and financial incentives in mHealth apps for medication adherence and to inform consensus-based design and policy considerations. <strong>Methods:</strong> A study was conducted using a modified virtual nominal group technique (vNGT). Nonpatient stakeholders across health care, industry, and policy sectors in Australia were recruited through purposive and convenience sampling between February and August 2025. Data collection involved a survey capturing demographics and initial perspectives, followed by online focus groups for consensus discussions. Qualitative responses were analyzed using thematic analysis supported by AI-assisted coding. Consensus statements derived from themes were rated during the focus groups. Additional probing prompts were used in the focus groups to encourage further discussion where consensus was not immediately achieved. Results from the focus groups were analyzed using descriptive statistics to summarize consensus ratings and discussions. <strong>Results:</strong> A total of 20 participants were included in the study. Nine participants reported having a health care professional background employment exclusively, while 11 reported having employment background across multiple sectors or exclusively outside health care. Six key themes were identified: tailored gamification for adherence, financial incentives as a contested motivator, designing for diversity and inclusion, usability barriers to engagement, trust through data governance, and validated and sustainable innovation. These informed 24 consensus statements, of which 54% (13/24) achieved unanimous agreement. Stakeholders strongly endorsed personalization, simplicity, and transparent data practices, while expressing nuanced concerns regarding the ethical use, sustainability, and potential unintended consequences of financial incentives. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Nonpatient stakeholders largely reinforce patient priorities while extending them with critical perspectives on implementation, governance, and sustainability. Gamification and financial incentives are viewed as potentially effective but require careful, ethically grounded design to balance engagement with long-term motivation and trust. These findings support the development of stakeholder-informed guidelines for responsible mHealth innovation and highlight the importance of integrating patient and system-level perspectives in digital health design. Future research should prioritize co-designed longitudinal studies using apps with gamification and a range of incentive offers with clear redemption processes to evaluate the long-term impact on medication adherence across diverse patient populations.
title: Nonpatient Stakeholder Perspectives on the Use of Gamification and Financial Incentives in Mobile Health for Medication Adherence: Modified Nominal Group Technique Study

summary: Meyer-Keirath and colleagues found no significant difference in posttreatment symptoms between video-based and face-to-face psychotherapy. However, the wide confidence interval indicates substantial imprecision, while the prediction interval suggests that comparative effects may vary considerably across settings; neither supports a conclusion of equivalence. For health services, symptom outcomes alone tell only part of the story. Future studies should report, by randomized group, who starts treatment, who discontinues it, and who completes the final assessment. These are distinct outcomes that may differ between delivery formats and affect the interpretation of symptom results. Video-based psychotherapy is a reasonable option, but its value should be assessed across the full treatment pathway. Adequately powered noninferiority trials should identify which patients can access, remain in, and benefit from each format.
title: Supporting Video-Based Psychotherapy While Asking Who Benefits and Who Remains in Treatment
